catalog_quote: 4.1 Stress. Stress is nonphonemic, occurring on the ultimate syllable only. When the penultimate syllable is lengthened, there is also a nonphonemic rising pitch on this vowel, the final stress being less pronounced. [ʔʌlɨkʌ́n] /ʔalɨkan/ 'to kiss'; [kʌla:ŋʌ́g] /kala:ŋag/ 'green parrot'. ... 4.3 Length with Vowels. Vowel length occurs frequently, especially with a. Contrasts are: /ga:bi/ 'taro root', /gabi/ 'night'; /na:ti/ 'colt', /nati/ 'baby deer'; /bi:tay/ 'hang up', /bitay/ 'up the hill'; /tu:d/ 'tree stump', /tud/ 'get'; /tu:bu/ 'pipe', /tubu/ 'sugar cane'; ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is automatic on the final syllable and not contrastive. What is contrastive is vowel length (at most one long vowel per word, typically the penult, e.g. ga:bi 'taro' vs gabi 'night'); a lengthened penult carries a rising pitch and weakens the final stress, so Dawson notes length could alternatively be analysed as an 'accent phoneme'. Root length shifts to stay penultimate under suffixation (si:paʔ, sipa:ʔin) and is removed by the long-vowel suffixes -a:nan/-i:nin/-u:nun; prefix ma:- keeps its length in or before the antepenult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; only the interaction noted above (lengthened penult with rising pitch makes the final stress 'less pronounced').
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions to final stress are given. For length: fn. 5 p. 54 /ka:lim/ 'want', /ka:liman/ 'wants' keeps root length under suffixation (vs /kalima:n/ 'fifty'); monosyllabic long roots shorten before -a:nan etc. (/ka:n/ 'eat', /kana:nan/); some short roots lengthen when suffixed (/teʔ/ 'sew', /te:ʔin/) or reduplicated (/kalug/, /kalugka:lug/).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonemic word (roots and affixed words up to six syllables, cited in isolation); stress explicitly treated as a word-level nonphonemic feature, length as phonemic. Fieldwork c. 1956-58, 18 months, two named male speakers from the Lumabat/Mainit river area beyond Malungon.
new_statements.identity_note: Dawson 1958 is titled 'Kalagan' and archive.org/Rosetta files it under ISO kqe, but the described variety is Tagakaulo (taga1268/klg): p. 47 places the fieldwork 'around the Lumabat and Mainit river areas, beyond Malungon, Cotabato' (Malungon is now in Sarangani Province, the Tagakaulo heartland per the Burtons' 1998 phrasebook preface), the speakers call the mountain dwellers 'Kalagan-Tagakolu', Gallman 1979:4-5 labels the Mainit data 'Kalagan-Tagakaolo (KLT)' citing Dawson 1958, SIL Philippines tags the Dawsons' 1955 Kalagan alphabet book as Tagakaulo [klg], and Glottolog files Dawson 1958 under taga1268. Not to be confused with kala1388 Kalagan [kqe] (Muslim Kalagan of Davao Oriental; Erkmann's 1993 phrasebook there says stress is usually penultimate) or kaga1255 Kagan Kalagan [kll] (Wendel & Wendel 1978).

sources.note: Sec. 4.1 Stress (p. 54): stress is nonphonemic and falls on the ultimate syllable only; when the penult is lengthened it carries a nonphonemic rising pitch and the final stress is weaker. Sec. 4.3 (p. 54-55): vowel length is contrastive (ga:bi 'taro' vs gabi 'night' etc.), occurs at most once per word and 'might be regarded as an accent phoneme'; some roots have inherent penult length, suffixes -a:nan/-i:nin/-u:nun remove root length, prefix ma:- keeps length in or before the antepenult.
